title: Congressional Address 2014 - "Finding Common Ground"
text:
Governor Calvo, Speaker Won Pat, Acting Chief Justice Carbullido, Distinguished Guests, and my dear people of Guam:
This past January, our island lost a great patriot, a distinguished statesman, a proud Marine, and a loyal son of Guam. Congressman Ben Blaz led an incredible life dedicated to service to our nation and our island. He was a trailblazer who inspired generations of Guamanians to work for something greater than themselves.
As a Congressman, Ben Blaz set an example as a leader who could set aside differences, commit to doing what is right for our people, and find common ground to improve the quality of life on this island that we all love.
It is in this spirit that I join you tonight to update you on my work in Congress and to discuss federal issues important to our island. I always appreciate the opportunity to come to the Legislature to make this annual address, but I hope in the near future that the Legislature will host speeches and events in a new Congress building. That building is an important symbol of Guam’s political history. I commend the Legislature for finding common ground and identifying funds to restore the historic Guam Congress building. Their efforts will ensure that future legislatures will meet in a building where our political history of self-governance had its beginnings.
Chamorro Culture 
The Guam Congress building, the new Guam Museum, the Hagatna restoration and many other efforts are being made to keep the Chamorro culture central to our island. We are at a critical period in our history where our ability to pass down our Chamorro heritage to our children hinges on the steps we take now. Our actions will determine whether our language and culture will survive well into the future. I believe that we are on the right track, and I commend the many efforts that are underway to ensure that Chamorro culture, history, and traditions are preserved.
Organizations like the Hurao Academy, Pa'a Taotao Tano, and  Inetnon Gef Pago are teaching our language and oral traditions. Our private sector is providing much-needed funding for these programs and many businesses and government agencies are taking the Hafa Adai Pledge. I commend the efforts of Senator Tommy Morrison for his efforts to re-instate Guam History and Chamorro Heritage Day. I commend Senator Tina Muna Barnes and Mr. Karl Pangelinan for being advocates of Chamorro culture through the Guam Visitors Bureau. Together our community is working to promote, protect, and pass down our island's cultural heritage. I will continue to do my part to support these efforts and ensure that federal resources are available for them. I hope that our community will continue to find common ground among all the rich cultures on Guam to enrich our future with our great past.  
Asia-Pacific Rebalance
The past year has seen significant progress regarding the military build-up on Guam, specifically the realignment of Marines from Okinawa and Air Force programs.  As Ranking Member of the Readiness Subcommittee, we found common ground with the Senate on the realignment.  Last year’s defense authorization bill lifted some of the most severe restrictions on the use of Government of Japan and U.S. military construction funds.  The Senate remained concerned over cost, but the lack of action on the U.S. had a significant impact on our bilateral relationship with the Government of Japan.  The compromise we reached allowed DoD to use Government of Japan funds for planning and design for any project on Guam and for construction projects located at Andersen Air Force Base to support the air element of a Marine Air-Ground Task Force.  The bill also authorized and appropriated over $85 million for a Marine Corps aircraft maintenance hangar on North Ramp which directly supports the realignment.  Although I would have preferred to eliminate the restrictions completely, the Senate continued to have concerns about the cost of the entire realignment, and the Navy has not yet completed its supplemental environmental impact statement.  The compromise allows us to move forward with some aspects of the realignment as we continue to address cost issues.  Moreover, we overcame strong objections of some U.S. Senators to the Air Force program at Andersen Force Base that hardens select infrastructure and disperses assets in the region.
Since the passage of the defense authorization bill, we have seen one of the most significant developments in the realignment of Marines on Okinawa after many years.  The Governor of Okinawa signed a landfill permit that allows the Government of Japan to begin the process of designing and constructing the landfill that is necessary to build a new Futenma Replacement Facility.  This event showed the commitment of Prime Minister Abe to moving forward with the realignment.
The President’s Budget for fiscal year 2015 contains $128 million in funding for Guam military infrastructure. That is a significant amount of investment in a year where the total military construction budget saw a 40 percent reduction from the previous year.  Our funding request underscores the Obama Administration’s commitment to the Asia-Pacific rebalance.  However, the budget environment in Washington remains very difficult.  While Congress did pass a two-year budget, we have not solved the problems of sequestration, and these cuts will return next year if Congress does not act. As such, I will work hard in this year’s defense bill to protect our funding and to eliminate all restrictions on Government of Japan funding.
On-going events in Syria and Ukraine may lead some people to question the validity of the Asia-Pacific rebalance strategy. However, Guam will continue to play a critical role for the United States in the Asia-Pacific region.  We are America’s forward presence in Asia, and we reassure our Asian allies that unlike Syria and Ukraine, the U.S. has forces at the ready and in the neighborhood to protect our interests. We must be mindful of the changing geopolitical dynamics and continue to advocate for our role in Asia. I commend our local leaders who convened a Guam-U.S.-Asia Security Alliance conference on Guam last year that provided the intellectual foundation for these policies. And I congratulate Juan Carlos Benitez, Carl Peterson and their team for organizing this successful conference.
Our role in Asia, however, puts Guam in a good position to avoid a base closure and realignment round, which the DoD is requesting.  But we must be mindful of the future. Last year I talked about how Guam and the Northern Marianas could become a hub for training activities for the U.S. military and our allies.  Building a robust regional training complex will be key to sustaining U.S. military capabilities on Guam and strengthen our case against a BRAC round.
We will get another opportunity to underscore our importance to U.S. posture in the region when the Navy releases its Supplemental E.I.S.  in the near future.  Our community will provide input on the realignment of Marines from Okinawa, specifically on where they will be housed and the location for a training range.  As has been publicly reported, we know that the Navy is looking at Northwest Field for the proposed firing range as well as existing DoD lands in Finegayan for the main base.  I was encouraged to see this news as I felt it directly responded to our community’s concerns several years ago.  The plan, as has been reported, does not require additional Government of Guam land and better utilizes existing DoD lands. 
During the previous E.I.S. some asked whether a firing range was needed on Guam.  Last June, the Secretary of Defense sent a certification to Congress indicating that a firing range on Guam is critical to maintaining military training and readiness of the U.S. Marine Corps.  If we want to host a Marine Air-Ground Task Force, then they need to be able to train on some basic requirements here on Guam.  The debate isn’t about whether a firing range is needed—because it is needed—but rather how do we accommodate this need while respecting the views of our community. Unfortunately, on an island with land constraints there are no perfect solutions, but I think the Navy is trying to be responsive to our fundamental concerns.  Groups such as We Are Guahan and Fuetsan Famalao'an have contributed to the discussion by raising the issue that Guam’s cultural resources must be protected. I also appreciate the continued efforts of the Guam Chamber of Commerce to highlight the positive economic impact of the realignment. The upcoming public forums on the Supplemental-E.I.S. will be an opportunity for all view points in our community to inform the Navy of our concerns so that this is done right for the military and for our community. If we want this realignment to happen, we must find common ground within our community on this important issue. And in finding common ground, our “One Guam” approach will have impact. I pledge to work with Governor Calvo, the Legislature and all of our stakeholders to find that common ground. 
The Supplemental E.I.S. will also highlight some of the infrastructure impacts the realignment will have on Guam, and it is important for our community to articulate and refine what these impacts are.  Another area where we found common ground with the Senate was the requirement for the Department of Defense to hold an Economic Adjustment Committee meeting this summer.  The objections in the Senate, led by Senator John McCain, over civilian infrastructure are well known.  I fought hard to protect civilian infrastructure funding, but the Senate was strongly opposed to the funding.  We have been successful in getting some civilian infrastructure funds spent like Defense Access Road funding and $50 million from the Maritime Administration for Port of Guam improvements.  I want to thank Senator Tom Ada for his oversight and leadership on matters of infrastructure and transportation programs here on Guam.  However, in an effort to move the broader civilian infrastructure issue forward and keep a continued DoD commitment, I felt it was appropriate to require DoD to hold another Economic Adjustment Committee meeting, as they did in 2009.  The Economic Adjustment Committee meeting will give Governor Calvo and local leaders an opportunity to review previous requests and make them more directly connected to the buildup.  Remember, we continue to operate in an environment dominated by fiscal conservatives, and asking DoD to fund civilian infrastructure is an easy target for budget cuts.  Reasonable requests tied to documented impacts and mitigations can help to minimize the objections. 
We don’t need to get our 10 priorities from on high. But we need to act together as a community to try to find common ground with the U.S. Senate who say we ask for too much instead of asking for things directly related to the military build-up.  We have to be reasonable in our requests and I hope that the E.A.C. will be more successful in getting other federal partners to support our needs and requirements.  At the end of the E.A.C. process I hope that we have more clarity on what are our civilian infrastructure needs and how we will get support from the federal government. 
Earlier this year, our island welcomed back nearly 600 of our National Guardsmen who participated in one of the largest deployments in our Guard’s history. These brave soldiers are true heroes who answered our nation’s call to serve, some of them for the second, third and fourth time. I want to particularly commend General Benny Paulino, Lieutenant Colonel Michael Tougher and Command Sergeant Major Melchor Hennegan for their leadership during this deployment.  We are proud of what each and every one of our National Guardsmen does in support of our nation and our island.
The difficult budget environment requires the Army and Air Force to make tough decisions.  There may be changes in the force structure and end strength of the Army and Air National Guard.  However, our National Guard here on Guam is one of the best in the country.  They have answered every call to serve, and it is that attitude that will make them invaluable in the future.  I will continue to work with them to establish a flying mission for our Air National Guard, and I look forward to receiving Light Utility Helicopters for our Army National Guard soon.  I will continue to fight for our Guam National Guard.
Last year, we saw a new and erratic leader in North Korea threaten very aggressive and hostile actions toward the United States, specifically Guam.  At the time, I encouraged DoD leadership to take aggressive steps to protect our people and position military assets on Guam, and they responded quickly.  While Guam had protection from an Aegis missile system in the Western Pacific, the deployment of a Terminal High Altitude Area Defense missile system provided direct protection from any missile threat from North Korea.  I commend the efforts of the DoD for their swift action in deploying the missile defense battery to Guam.  I want to recognize Brigadier General Steven Garland, Commander of the 36th Wing and Lieutenant Colonel Clyde Cochrane, Commander Task Force Talon for their leadership in the Defense of Guam Mission.
I will continue to work with Army leadership and the Joint Chiefs to find solutions to keep the missile defense battery stationed here on Guam for the long-term.  Last week, at the annual Army budget hearing, I questioned General Odierno about the long-term stationing of a missile defense battery on Guam.  I appreciated his comment that the Army is working with the Joint Chiefs to find a solution to keep it here on Guam.  The missile defense battery remains an important deterrent to adversaries in the region.
Veterans 
While we recognize the efforts of current servicemembers, we cannot lose focus on the service and sacrifice of our veterans.  One of the initiatives to assist with this is the establishment of a Veteran’s Court at the Guam Judiciary. I am encouraged by the leadership of Senator Frank Aguon Jr., former Chief Justice Phil Carbullido, Presiding Judge Alberto Lamorena and the Guam VA Administrator John Unpingco in exploring the viability of setting up a Veteran’s Court. Last year, I challenged our local leaders to take on this initiative, and I will do my part to find federal funding to assist them in this endeavor. A Veteran’s court recognizes the important contributions of our veterans and provides alternatives that will help them get past their brush with the law.
Last year, I joined Congressman Jeff Miller, the Chairman of the House Veterans Affairs Committee, and other members of the House Veterans Affairs and Armed Services Committees, on a Congressional Delegation that visited Guam. We listened to the concerns of our community, and I continue to work with Congressional leaders to address challenges we face. One area where we have seen progress is in the expansion of the Guam Veterans Cemetery. In September, the VA announced that it would be investing $3.2 million to add an additional 2,000 gravesites to the cemetery and I commend John Unpingco on his work on this grant.
We must also work to ensure that our veterans have access to quality health care. I understand the VA is currently conducting a comprehensive review of VA services in Guam and the Pacific area to develop a long term plan to improve health care access for local veterans. I continue to push for the VA to move forward with funding a $4.4 million expansion project to the community based outpatient clinic that I was successful in placing on their integrated list of construction priorities. I am encouraged that the VA is addressing staffing issues at the clinic.  They recently brought on another full-time physician and they are offering tele-health primary care services with the VA system in Hawaii. 
In caring for our veterans, we must make an extra effort to address homeless veterans on Guam. I commend the efforts of our non-profit community in partnering with WestCare and our local VA office to apply for federal grants that support programs to reduce or eliminate veteran homelessness. 
We honor those in our active duty, guard and reserve who have answered our nation’s call. But above all we honor those who have died to protect our freedom. We remember the 23 men and women who gave their lives in service to our nation in Iraq and Afghanistan.  They paid the ultimate sacrifice to defend our freedom and liberties, and we will always remember them.
War Claims
In a similar way, we must never forget the incredible sacrifices and hardships borne by our man’amko who endured 32 months of brutal enemy occupation during World War II. In my Congressional Address last year, I told you that I had proposed an offset to the costs of paying war claims that would satisfy the budget objections raised by fiscal conservatives in Congress. I worked with my colleagues to include this provision in the Omnibus Territories Act that has been introduced in both the House and Senate. Last month, the Congressional Budget Office scored this offset, and determined that it meets the most stringent test of both Chambers’ budget rules.  I commend Senator Rory Respicio for working with me to ensure support in the Guam Legislature for our war claims budget offset and for his tireless work on federal issues.   
Yet despite finding an offset that is budget neutral, and satisfying every other concern that has been raised by conservatives in Congress, passing war claims continues to be a difficult task. The truth is, many conservatives will continue to object to this bill on purely ideological grounds and no arguments of moral obligation or social injustice will change their views. But I pledge to you, that I will continue to fight so that our man'amko receive the recognition they justly deserve. General Blaz put it perfectly during a hearing of the House Natural Resources Committee in 2011 when he said, "Mr. Chairman, if you don’t remember anything else that I have to say is that, sir, we are not trying to get this compensation to bring back the dead. All we are trying is to get this compensation to honor the living." It is our duty to do all that we can to finally resolve this longstanding injustice.
Every year we honor the Liberation of Guam with a wreath laying ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery and a Congressional Reception on Capitol Hill.  I appreciate the support of the Governor’s Office, the Mayors Council of Guam, the Guam Visitors Bureau, the Guam Chamber of Commerce and many local businesses who help to make these events possible. Next year we are commemorating the 70th Anniversary of the Liberation of Guam and I hope that some of our local leaders and will be able to join us for this commemoration.
Economy
Of great importance to our community is the strength of our economy.  I was encouraged to see that our once high unemployment rate of 13.3% dropped to 10.7% back in December.  While not perfect this figure shows progress in the right direction.  I commend the efforts of Governor Calvo in working with the bond market to improve our bond rating which grants us better rates and access to more capital.  This is only accomplished if there is evidence of future economic growth and expansion.  To that end, I continue to work closely with Governor Calvo, the Legislature and our visitor industry to expand our visa waiver program.  We continue to work through security concerns that some federal agencies have with expanding the program to Chinese tourists.  As I stated last year, I believe there are reasonable and workable mitigations to their concerns.  I am encouraged to see new leadership at Department of Defense and the Department of Homeland Security, and I look forward to continuing to work with them on this critical issue for our island’s tourism industry.  Expansion of our tourism industry is critical, along with a military build-up, to providing economic opportunities for our people. I just learned of an effort to add Vietnam to the list of visa waiver countries that can visit Guam, and I want to add my support to this promising proposal. And we continue to try to overcome objections to our request to add the Philippines to the Guam visa waiver program.
Another important pillar of our economy is maintaining a robust depot level ship repair capability on Guam.  The Navy devised an acquisition strategy that separates our ship repair work on Guam into three components.  The first element is a contract for pierside work on Navy and MSC vessels.  I congratulate Cabras Marine for winning that contract, and look forward to them beginning full operations out of the former Ship Repair Facility on Navy Base Guam.  The second part of the strategy is to charter a dry-dock followed by another contract for work to be performed on ships in the dry-dock.
Having a dry-dock on Guam is critical to maintaining a depot level capability – a capability that we have fought for years to develop and maintain.  I will continue to urge the Navy to maintain this capability as a national asset and to preserve highly skilled jobs on Guam.  A robust depot level ship repair capability is critical to our Navy’s readiness in the Western Pacific.  Both Admiral Locklear and Admiral Greenert agree with my assertions and have agreed to work with me to maintain this capability on Guam. 
I will also continue to support efforts to enhance the capabilities of the workforce. I am encouraged to see that Cabras Marine has established an apprenticeship program and is looking to enhance the capabilities of their workforce.  That is absolutely what we need employers on Guam to do to grow our economy.  Cabras Marine is doing the right thing by investing in our people now through training programs.
Last month, President Obama submitted his budget proposal to Congress. One of his initiatives to help the middle class is to expand the earned income tax credit. While there have already been objections raised by other Members of Congress to this proposal, we cannot ignore the possibility that Congress is expected to make reforms to the federal tax code in the coming years. Guam's mirror tax code could be significantly affected by changes to Internal Revenue Code, and we cannot rely on fiscal conservatives in Congress to provide funding for every change to the code that's meant to improve tax policy at the national level.
I believe the Guam Legislature can provide leadership in exploring delinking from the internal revenue code so we can make our own tax decisions that reflect what is best for Guam and not rely on mandates that are meant for the nation as a whole. We already have this authority, and it is within the power of the Legislature and the Governor to enter into an agreement with the Internal Revenue Service for this purpose. I appreciate the efforts of Senators Mike Limtiaco and Mike San Nicolas to explore this issue, and I hope that we can set in motion a plan that gives Guam its own tax code that promotes growth.
You cannot have a growing economy without ensuring public safety.  I commend Lieutenant Governor Ray Tenorio, Chief Fred Bordallo and the Guam Police Department for the great strides they are making to keep our community safe.  I acknowledge the work of our federal and local judiciary, led by Chief Judge Frances Tydingco-Gatewood and Chief Justice Robert Torres.  I also commend our U.S. Attorney Alicia Limtiaco and our Attorney General Lenny Rapadas for their effective leadership of their federal and local law enforcement agencies. And I commend Senator Tony Ada for his focus on new laws that will make us safe in our homes and safe in our community.
These efforts to build our economy are focused on building a better Guam, and in my view, a better Guam is a Guam without casino gambling. In recent years, outside interests have come to our island and have poured a lot of money into Guam to convince us that casino gambling is a good bet for our future. Seven times in a row, our people, by a two-thirds margin, have said no, and please go away. Our people are tired of the constant barrage by pro-casino outside interests. We have said enough is enough, båsta and no more.  I will introduce legislation, called the Båsta Act, which will finally put an end to this cycle. The Båsta Act amends the Johnson Act to level the playing field. If enacted, the Båsta Act would mean that casinos cannot be established without local and federal approval. No longer will casino interests be able to use our local laws to impose their values on us. I will continue to work with local leaders and community partners to reject casino gambling once and for all.  I want to recognize Senators BJ Cruz, Ben Pangelinan, and Mike San Nicolas for their leadership in opposing casino gambling on Guam.  It’s time that we all say – båsta!
Compact Impact 
However we cannot fully discuss ways to improve our economy without addressing the effects the Compacts of Free Association have on our community. We first should acknowledge the many positive contributions that Compact migrants have on our community. While I continue to support the intent of the Compacts and understand the benefits these agreements have for our nation, the reality is that our local government cannot continue to bear the current costs for providing social services to Compact migrants. While we continue to push the federal government to increase its Compact assistance, given the fiscal challenges in Washington, we must find alternative solutions that contribute to a more sustainable policy.
I commend Vice Speaker Cruz for his leadership in finding ways to remove Compact migrants who have been convicted of crimes on Guam back to their home countries, in accordance with federal immigration laws. Senator Cruz has uncovered inconsistent enforcement of the federal deportation laws and I will work with him to correct this failure of enforcement.  I also hope to build on the progress Vice Speaker Cruz has made by working with the Governor, the Legislature, and the Judiciary to formulate local policies and amend local laws that would make alternative sentencing an option for the courts.  Guam's prison is beyond its maximum capacity, and giving the courts the means to authorize FAS migrants convicted of non-violent offenses to serve their terms in their own country will help to alleviate the overcrowding at the Guam Department of Corrections.  I hope the Guam Legislature will provide leadership and work with Chief Justice Torres and the legal community to give judges discretion with alternative sentences for appropriate offenses. We should explore alternative sentencing, along with federal deportations, as ways to reduce the Compact migrant population at the Guam prison.
I commend Senator Brant McCreadie for his efforts to call attention to the conditions at the prison and for offering a solution to the overcrowding. I will help him by supporting federal funding to help with the construction of a new prison.  
This is not to say that everything must be done at the local level. I continue to advocate for ways to lessen the financial strain Compact migrants have placed on the Government of Guam. Last year I included a provision in the Omnibus Territories Act that would allow GovGuam to offset matching requirements for federal programs with the amount GovGuam has spent to provide social services to Compact migrants. Although the Obama Administration objected to this provision, I will work with Interior to resolve their concerns. I believe that this is a viable option that could significantly benefit our community. 
However one of the key setbacks to analyzing how to move forward with addressing Compact impact is the lack of guidance from Interior on how the affected jurisdictions are to accurately account for the true costs of these services. The U.S. Government Accountability Office underscored this point in their study on the Compacts, and I have consistently urged the Interior Department to develop such a metric. I have also urged the Senate to confirm President Obama’s nominee for Assistant Secretary of the Interior for Insular Areas, Ms. Esther Kia’aina. We need strong leadership at the Office of Insular Affairs to focus on all our issues, particularly Compact-impact, and to help us make the case for additional funding in the President’s budget.
Education 
As we continue look for common ground to build a more robust economy, we must also ensure that we are preparing our children for the future. I have been encouraged by the incredible progress made at Guam DOE, the Guam Community College, and the University of Guam to improve the quality of education for our students.
Through the leadership of Superintendent Jon Fernandez, Dr. Mary Okada, and Dr. Robert Underwood, the Department of Education has implemented Guam’s first Science, Technology, Engineering and Math, or STEM, program. Our education leaders literally found common ground at my alma mater, George Washington High School.  GW now houses classrooms that have been upgraded to support STEM education for our secondary school children. Their work is just the first step in developing this program for all our students. Senator Aline Yamashita has been a champion for education reform and we acknowledge her leadership in helping to implement the STEM program.
I commend Superintendent Fernandez and his team at Guam DOE for working with Governor Calvo, the Guam Legislature, the U.S. Department of Education, the Office of Insular Affairs, and my office to leverage federal resources available to Guam. Their efforts were instrumental to ensuring that Guam did not lose funding provided by the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, and because of them, our public school system has benefited from millions of dollars in federal investments. For example, renovations like Southern High School’s fine arts auditorium and gymnasium are prime examples of local and federal leaders finding common ground to improve education for our public school children. Further I am proud of the progress that has been made at Untalan Middle School since I visited the school in 2010. Untalan is a model of utilizing Recovery Act funding to repair schools in our community and I look forward to its reopening.
Beyond bricks and concrete, I will support the efforts of the Guam Education Policy Board and Superintendent Fernandez to find ways to more accurately promote and measure student progress in the classroom.
I commend Dr. Mary Okada for her leadership in using federal funds to transform the Guam Community College into a first class campus on Guam, and building capacity to participate in President Obama’s College to Career Initiative. This initiative partners community colleges with businesses to better transition from classrooms to our workforce. Further, GCC’s participation in the TRIO program has helped many disadvantaged students obtain a college education. I will continue to work with GCC’s leadership to ensure that we make the most of federal funding available for improvement of curriculum and facilities.
I also recognize Dr. Robert Underwood and the leadership of UOG as they develop the university’s role as a leading and innovative institution in the Asia Pacific Region. UOG has been a leader in facilitating scientific research in our region, and plays a key role in the climate change battle we face. Under Dr. Underwood’s leadership, UOG has also made important strides in partnering with universities across Asia to expand the classroom experience, enhance research and create economic opportunities for Guam. This will place UOG at the nexus of our region, and grow our influence among our fellow Pacific Island and Asian partners.
Superintendent Fernandez, Dr. Underwood, and Dr. Okada have all found common ground to significantly improve the quality of education on Guam. I will continue to do my part to support their efforts and ensure that our children are well prepared for the future.  
Health Care 
In February, I joined my colleagues and the Governors from the territories in sitting down with federal officials during a meeting of the Interagency Group on Insular Areas to discuss the many challenges facing our islands. A major topic of discussion was the Affordable Care Act, and the challenges facing Guam’s insurance providers as they move toward implementation. I recognize that the Affordable Care Act is an imperfect law, especially as it applies to the territories, but we must find ways to make it work on Guam so that our people may benefit and live healthier lives.
One proposal to leverage the resources provided to Guam through the Affordable Care Act is for GovGuam to apply for a waiver from the Department of Health and Human Services that would allow Guam to use funds authorized for Medicaid to help individuals purchase private insurance. As many of you will recall, the Affordable Care Act provided Guam with an additional $268 million for Medicaid, much of which we have not been able to draw down because of the lack of local resources to meet federal matching requirements. Similar Medicaid waivers have already been approved for Arkansas, Iowa, and Pennsylvania. HHS has committed to working with Guam Public Health to ensure that this waiver authority will benefit our community. Further during the Interagency Group on Insular Areas meeting, HHS announced that Guam is eligible for a temporary increase in our Federal Medical Assistance Program ratio. I commend Tess Archangel at Guam Public Health for working with HHS to secure this temporary increase. Further, I appreciate the work of Senator Dennis Rodriguez for bringing together our government agencies and community stakeholders to discuss how the Affordable Care Act impacts Guam and possible solutions moving forward.
I will also continue to work with Governor Calvo, the Legislature, and our insurers to mitigate the challenges the Affordable Care Act is having on our community. I support asking the Centers for Medicaid and Medicaid Services to revisit the essential health benefits plan currently enforced on Guam, and I will work with my colleagues from the territories to find ways to improve the application of the Affordable Care Act in our communities. While the Affordable Care Act extends consumer protections to our residents, it did not extend the employer and individual mandates or provide funds for premium tax credits. In effect it left to the Legislature to decide whether or not we want to have employer or individual mandates or tax incentives. I will continue to work with our insurance stakeholders and leaders to determine if benefits we receive are not undermined by the very real possibility insurance rates will skyrocket. The heart of this issue is that while insurance providers can no longer reject applicants with pre-existing conditions, they would not have the benefit of an expanded insurance pool without the individual and employer mandates. This has been the warning from our insurance providers and we need to find ways to make the economic realities work on Guam.
I have joined the territorial delegates in raising concerns with HHS and the administration. I am sensitive to the concerns of the insurance providers, and I am working with them to get the answers they need, or as an alternative, create local policies that will make the consumer protections economically viable. I will continue to work the Governor, Senator Rodriguez, and the insurance providers on this issue.
Environment 
To protect our island heritage, we must be responsible and innovative in our use and management of our environment and our natural resources for future generations. The issue of invasive species remains a challenging one for our community, from brown tree snakes to the coconut rhinoceros beetle to fire ants. I commend the efforts of Senator Chris Duenas for looking for ways for GovGuam to better address invasive species, and I commit to working with him to find federal resources to address these challenging issues.
I will also continue to closely monitor the reauthorization of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act. The Magnuson-Stevens Act protects our fisheries, prohibits foreign fishing fleets from our waters, and helps rebuild fish stocks. We must wisely manage these resources, carefully balancing conservation with the economic impacts to our fishermen.  The Western Pacific Fisheries Management Council and the Guam Fisherman’s Co-op are partners in our efforts to make the Magnuson-Stevenson reforms more responsive to our local fishermen.  I also continue to work for passage of my bill to address illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing because this activity by foreign fleets is harming our region’s economy, ecosystems and security.
You may have heard the old adage: Give a man fish, he’ll eat for a day. Teach a man to fish, and he’ll have food for a lifetime. To that I would add the Bordallo Amendment: Punish a man for stealing the fish out of your waters, and you will ensure you have enough fish to fish for a lifetime.
Political Status
Tonight, we have covered many issues affecting Guam and the ways we can find common ground to ensure that we are leaving our island better for our children. However, we cannot satisfy our obligations to our children if we do not work to resolve Guam’s political status. Over the years, we have made progress in moving this process along, but more work remains. I commend Governor Calvo, Speaker Won Pat, and Vice Speaker Cruz for their work to empanel the Commission on Decolonization. I understand that the Commission is working to submit a proposal to the Office of Insular Affairs for an education campaign to educate our people on the self-determination process. I will work with Interior to ensure that Guam receives federal assistance needed for this process, and I hope the Commission will submit this consolidated grant proposal soon.
In my view, self-determination is the most important long-term goal for our island. Undoubtedly there are differences in how self-determination should move forward, but we must find common ground to finally move the process along. I commend Senator Pangelinan for his work to develop the Chamorro registry. I believe the Chamorro vote is a critical step in the process, but it is not the only step. Self-determination will include our whole community, but we cannot deny the rights of our indigenous people to have their say in how they want to see our island move forward. I am confident that as we go forward with this process, we will be able to find common ground so that the views of our indigenous people will be respected and the voices of all Guam’s residents will be heard. 
Finding Common Ground
It has again been my honor to make this report to our people. While we have overcome many challenges in the past year and found success on some federal issues, we continue to work on other issues that may be more difficult.  Our federal government and Congress have seen many changes.  The new normal is a federal budget that is shrinking while our obligations continue to grow. Extremists in Congress have shown that they would rather shut down the federal government than make tough compromises – in the end, reason and compromises won the day.  We face the same challenges but we have one big advantage – we don’t hate each other. We respect each other and we recognize that differences of opinion or differing policies do not make us enemies.  We will always be neighbors, friends, and relatives and we will always share Guam as our common ground.
Thank you, Maraming Salamat Po and Dangkulo na Si Yu’os Ma’ase.  May God Bless Guam and May God Bless the United States of America.

title: Rep. Schock Testifies On Rejected Design for Eisenhower Memorial
text:
Washington, D.C. – In public testimony today before the National Capital Planning Commission, Rep. Aaron Schock (IL-18) voiced opposition to the current design for the Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial, calling the controversial proposal “incoherent” and “confusing.” The present design includes, among other contentious elements: a series of large scale columns measuring 80’ tall and 10’ in diameter; three stainless steel tapestries as large as 447 feet long and 80 feet high; and a statue of President Eisenhower as a bare-footed boy. Schock has long opposed the present design, which was rejected today by a 7-3 majority of the Commission’s bipartisan members.  
Contrasting the proposed Eisenhower Memorial – which was designed by California-based architect Frank Gehry – with the Lincoln Memorial, Schock noted that the Gehry design “does not lead us to any conclusion about the great man honored. Rather, it seems that the current design’s sole purpose is to lead us to a conclusion about the designer himself.”  
“The Gehry proposal,” Schock continued, “is a four acre theme park without a coherent theme.”  
In his remarks, Schock reminded Commissioners that the Eisenhower family opposes the current design, also unlike the Lincoln Memorial that was dedicated by President Lincoln’s sole-surviving son, Robert Todd Lincoln, in 1922.
“I would hope – that should any of us in this room rise to the esteemed place in history that President Eisenhower did – our families would be as committed to a fitting tribute for us as the Eisenhower family have been for him.”  
Schock, whose district includes many of the counties formerly represented by President Lincoln during his single House term, testified at today’s hearing at the invitation of numerous constituents who have been concerned that the Eisenhower Memorial design did not convey the majesty or reflect the legacy of President Eisenhower.
Video archives and photographs from Schock’s testimony will be available later at schock.house.gov and at https://www.youtube.com/user/CongressmanSchock.
Remarks for the National Capital Planning Commission
Congressman Aaron Schock (IL-18)
April 3, 2014  
Mr. Chairman, Commissioners, ladies and gentlemen.  
Thank you for the opportunity to discuss some aspects of the proposed Eisenhower Memorial and whether it will complement our nation’s core and reflect the legacy of our great general and President.  
The designer of the proposed memorial, Frank Gehry, has said that he likes the Lincoln Memorial, which includes an immense statue inside an inspiring building. 
I hope that we all have had the experience of approaching that monument, viewing the colonnade around the memorial, the great staircase, the entrance columns that bring us into the memorial itself.  
And then, to stand before the seated Lincoln and see the pains of war, the virtue, the wisdom apparent in his eyes.  
It is a progression of sights and experiences that end in the statue – flanked by the words of the Great Emancipator himself.  We are engaged by his place in history and called to reflect on our own.  
The proposed Eisenhower Memorial does not lead us to any conclusion about the great man honored. Rather, it seems that the current designs sole purpose is to lead us to a conclusion about the designer himself.
The proposed sculptures are confusing:  a young man looking down on the park; a General with a group of others in uniform, and a President looking at a globe.   
One must wonder if this is a memorial park rather than a memorial.  The chaos of the chain link fences and the columns and stacks of arbitrarily placed concrete blocks do not convey the majesty of President Eisenhower.  
In sum, the Gehry proposal is a four-acre theme park without a coherent theme. 
I note, as you have, the opposition of the Eisenhower family to the Gehry design. I would hope – that should any of us in this room rise to the esteemed place in history that President Eisenhower did – our families would be as committed to a fitting tribute for us as the Eisenhower family has been for him.”  
I support efforts to reject this design.  I urge the Eisenhower Memorial Commission to hold a new competition – one open to all Americans, and not a select few modernists.  A free and open competition will doubtlessly generate an appropriate Eisenhower memorial that will be a credit to the great man, and an attractive complement to our National Mall.
###

title: Corker, Colleagues Seek Answers from Administration on Internet Transition
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Bob Corker (R-Tenn.) yesterday joined Senators John Thune (R-S.D.), Marco Rubio (R-Fla.) and 32 of their Senate Republican colleagues in sending a letter to the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), seeking clarification regarding the recent announcement that NTIA intends to relinquish responsibility of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) functions, the system for assigning website addresses, to the global multistakeholder community.
“With the Internet playing an increasingly critical role in providing economic and educational opportunity for Americans as well as powerfully promoting liberty abroad, the United States must ensure the Internet remains free and open, and out of the hands of foreign governments or bad actors,” Corker said.
The letter expresses strong support for “the existing bottom-up, multistakeholder approach to Internet governance,” and cautions that we “must not allow the IANA functions to fall under the control of repressive governments, America’s enemies, or unaccountable bureaucrats.” 
The letter goes on to say, “The global community of Internet stakeholders should act deliberately and transparently as it formulates a possible proposal to transition the IANA functions to a nongovernmental entity. The multistakeholder model of Internet governance and the IANA functions are far too important for this process to be rushed or to be done behind closed doors.”
Among other things, the letter asks the administration to “explain why it is in our national interest to transition the IANA functions,” whether this transition can take place unilaterally “without an Act of Congress,” and how NTIA will ensure “the IANA functions do not end up being controlled, directly or indirectly, by a government or inter-governmental entity.”
Thune, Rubio, and Corker were joined by Senators Kelly Ayotte (R-N.H.), John Barrasso (R-Wyo.), Roy Blunt (R-Mo.), John Boozman (R-Ark.), Richard Burr (R-N.C.), Saxby Chambliss (R-Ga.), Dan Coats (R-Ind.), Tom Coburn (R-Okla.), John Cornyn (R-Texas), Mike Crapo (R-Idaho), Ted Cruz (R-Texas), Mike Enzi (R-Wyo.), Deb Fischer (R-Neb.), Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), Orrin Hatch (R-Utah), Dean Heller (R-Nev.), John Hoeven (R-N.D.), Jim Inhofe (R-Okla.), Mike Johanns (R-Neb.), Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), Mark Kirk (R-Ill.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), John McCain (R-Ariz.), Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), Jerry Moran (R-Kan.), Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Rob Portman (R-Ohio), Jim Risch (R-Idaho), Pat Roberts (R-Kan.), Tim Scott (R-S.C.), David Vitter (R-La.), and Roger Wicker (R-Miss.).
Full text of the letter is included below and available online here.
The Honorable Lawrence Strickling  Assistant Secretary for Communications and Information  National Telecommunications and Information Administration  U.S. Department of Commerce  1401 Constitution Avenue, N.W.  Washington, DC 20230 
Dear Assistant Secretary Strickling:
We write concerning the recent announcement by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) that it intends to relinquish responsibility of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) functions to the global multistakeholder community.  In its announcement, NTIA also asked the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) to convene stakeholders and develop a proposal to transition the role currently played by NTIA. 
We strongly support the existing bottom-up, multistakeholder approach to Internet governance that has led to immense prosperity and empowerment for individuals around the world.  The current approach has helped to define the open Internet, which has allowed the private sector to deliver technology and services that have changed our lives for the better.  In 2012, many of us were leaders on S. Con. Res. 50, a resolution that reinforced the U.S. government’s opposition to ceding control of the Internet to the International Telecommunications Union (ITU), an arm of the United Nations, or to any other governmental body.  As you know, S. Con. Res. 50 unanimously passed both the Senate and the House of Representatives, a rare instance of bipartisan agreement on such an important topic.
In announcing the intended transition, NTIA committed that it “will not accept a proposal that replaces the NTIA role with a government-led or an inter-governmental organization solution.”  We agree that any such proposal would be completely unacceptable.  Replacing NTIA’s role with another governmental organization would be disastrous, and we would vigorously oppose such a plan.  We must not allow the IANA functions to fall under the control of repressive governments, America’s enemies, or unaccountable bureaucrats.
The global community of Internet stakeholders should act deliberately and transparently as it formulates a possible proposal to transition the IANA functions to a nongovernmental entity.  The multistakeholder model of Internet governance and the IANA functions are far too important for this process to be rushed or to be done behind closed doors.
Because this issue is so important to the future of the Internet and for the protection of American values and interests, we request expeditious responses to the following questions and requests for information about the proposed IANA transition.
 
A 2000 report by the U.S. General Accounting Office stated that “it is unclear if the Department [of Commerce] has the requisite authority” to transfer control of the IANA functions to a private entity.  Please provide us with the Administration’s legal views and analysis on whether the United States Government can transition the IANA functions to another entity without an Act of Congress.
 
 
Please explain why it is in our national interest to transition the IANA functions to the “global multistakeholder community.” 
 
 
You have stated that NTIA believes “the timing is right to start the transition process.”  Why does the Administration believe now is the appropriate time to begin the transition, and what was the specific circumstance or development that led the Administration to decide to begin the transition now?
 
 
What steps will NTIA take to ensure the process to develop a transition plan for the IANA functions is open and transparent?
 
 
Will NTIA actively participate in the global multistakeholder process to develop a transition plan for the IANA functions, or will the Administration leave the process entirely in the hands of ICANN?
 
 
You have stated that NTIA “will not accept a proposal that replaces NTIA’s role with a government-led or an inter-governmental solution,” but NTIA has been silent on how it will ensure the IANA functions do not end up being controlled, directly or indirectly, by a government or inter-governmental entity.  What specific options are available to NTIA to prevent this from happening?
 
 
How can the Administration guarantee the multistakeholder organization that succeeds NTIA will not subsequently transfer the IANA functions to a government or intergovernmental organization in the future, or that such successor organization will not eventually fall under the undue influence of other governments?
 
 
NTIA asked ICANN to lead the transition process.  However, ICANN has a potential self-interest in increasing its own autonomy and reducing its accountability to other entities.  Some stakeholders have expressed concerns that ICANN may seek to control the IANA functions on its own, without oversight from anyone else.  How did NTIA determine that ICANN is the appropriate entity to lead the transition process, and how will NTIA ensure that ICANN does not inappropriately control or influence the process for its own self-interest? 
 
 
Does NTIA believe ICANN currently is sufficiently transparent and accountable in its activities, or should ICANN adopt additional transparency and accountability requirements as part of the IANA transition? 
 
 
Is it realistic to expect that an acceptable transition plan can be developed before the IANA functions contract expires on September 30, 2015?  Is there another example of a similar global stakeholder transition plan being developed and approved in just 18 months?  
 
 
How will NTIA ultimately decide whether a proposed transition plan for IANA, developed by global stakeholders, is acceptable?  What factors will NTIA use to determine if such a proposal supports and enhances the multistakeholder model; maintains the security, stability, and resiliency of the Internet Domain Name System; meets the needs and expectation of the global customers and partners of the IANA services; and maintains the openness of the Internet? 
 
 
Will NTIA also take into account American values and interests in evaluating a proposed transition plan? How? 
 
As this process moves forward, we will conduct careful oversight on behalf of the American people to ensure that American values, American interests, and the open Internet are protected.  Your detailed responses to our questions and requests for information will aid in that oversight, and we thank you in advance for your personal attention to this matter. 
Sincerely,
###

title: Corker: 150,000 Killed in Syria, Still No Strategy from the Obama Administration
text:
WASHINGTON – A week after a senior State Department official agreed to discuss with senators in a non-public setting the U.S. contingency plans for Syria, including military options and support for the Syrian opposition, U.S. Senator Bob Corker (R-Tenn.), ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said no briefing has been setup, leaving him to conclude that the Obama administration has no strategy for Syria even as the death toll in the conflict topped 150,000 this week.
“A week after administration officials stonewalled our committee, making reckless statements about U.S. contingencies for Syria that don’t appear to exist, we still have not had the briefing we were promised, leading me to conclude the administration has no Syrian strategy,” said Corker. “Without a coherent Syria policy from day one, the administration has contributed to the worsening conflict through inaction, limiting our options, diminishing U.S. credibility and putting U.S. interests and our country’s security at risk.  Members on both sides of the aisle are demanding answers, and I will continue to press the administration until we get them.”
At a Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing last Wednesday on U.S. policy in Syria after the failure of Geneva peace talks, Chairman Robert Menendez (D-N.J.) and Ranking Member Corker requested a closed briefing from the administration after State Department officials refused to answer some of the committee’s questions about U.S. involvement in Syria stating the answers were classified information.
Top U.S. intelligence officials have said the conflict in Syria now threatens the U.S. homeland.
###

title: CONGRESSWOMAN LORETTA SANCHEZ QUESTIONS ARMY AND MARINE CORPS ABOUT GROUND SYSTEM MODERNIZATION PROGRAMS
text:
WASHINGTON – Congresswoman Loretta Sanchez (CA-46), senior member of the House Armed Services Committee and Ranking Member of the Tactical Air and Land Forces Subcommittee, yesterday questioned officials at a hearing of the Tactical Air and Land Forces Subcommittee entitled "Fiscal Year 2015 Ground Force Modernization Programs." Below is her opening statement as prepared for delivery as well as a question she asked regarding costs of body armor.
CLICK HERE TO WATCH THE FULL HEARING
“Today’s hearing will cover Army and Marine Corps ground system modernization programs. This is a broad range of topics, covering everything from individual equipment such as body armor up to Abrams tanks or Stryker vehicles. However, within this broad range the Fiscal Year 2015 budget does show some general trends, many of which are troubling:
 
“First, it is clear that modernization for Army and Marine Corps ground equipment is under serious budget pressure and is becoming a bill payer for both services’ overall budget shortfalls. With only a few exceptions, almost every major program in this area has been scaled back, delayed, or terminated, in large part due to a lack of funding.
 
“For example, the Army is terminating the Ground Combat Vehicle program, delaying its high priority tactical network programs, dramatically scaling back wheeled vehicle upgrades, and slowing down production of Apache attack helicopters.
 
“For the Marines, purchases of new Joint Light Tactical Vehicles are delayed, the Amphibious Combat Vehicle program is being scaled back, and there is very little new investment in most areas.
 
“Second, there is a worrying trend in both services’ ability to actually field new systems through the normal acquisition process. In the area of large scale, acquisition category 1 programs continue to start with much fanfare, and then end up being terminated due to cost growth, changing priorities, or shifting service requirements.
 
“In addition, constantly changing senior service leadership priorities appear to be making it very difficult for the respective service acquisition officials to keep programs funded in the budget long enough to actually get new capabilities to the field. As a result, both the Army and Marine Corps keep pouring funding into new programs that don’t get across the finish line.
 
“There are numerous examples.  In the Army, the termination of the Ground Combat Vehicle is the most recent example.  The Army has once again spent more than a billion dollars and not gotten anything to the field. The Marine Corps has spent more than $3 billion over 20 years trying to field a vehicle to replace the current amphibious assault vehicle, but still hasn’t gotten anything new to our Marines.
 
“Third, the disturbing trend of needless duplication between Army and Marine Corps equipment continues. To name a few, both the Marine Corps and the Army are working on separate multi-mission radar systems, separate precision mortar rounds, and separate 120mm tank ammunition. The Army and Marine Corps also don’t use the same helicopters despite obvious similarities between the missions conducted by the two helicopter fleets.
 
“One specific example of this is the fact that the Army, Air Force, and Navy all use UH-60 “Blackhawk” helicopters of various models, but the Marine Corps continues to request hundreds of millions for upgrades to its aging fleet of H-1 helicopters.
 
“While Army and Marine Corps duplication may sometimes be appropriate, in the future the two services must find a way to have more joint programs so we can minimize waste and inefficiency inherent in maintaining separate inventories of equipment in each service.
 
“However, it is important to keep a few areas of relative success in mind.
 
“In the area of body armor and protective equipment, for example, both the Army and Marine Corps now have well-established research and development efforts and a healthy inventory of high-quality equipment.
 
“I remain concerned, however, about the ability of both services to maintain these investments in soldier and marine protection equipment as their overall budgets come under more pressure.
 
“Both services have also done a good job with keeping the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle program on track. That program is, as of now, a model of how competition, stable requirements, and thorough testing can lead to a successful acquisition program.
 
I look forward to today’s hearing and yield back.”
 
The Congresswoman also asked the following question: 
 
“Last year Congress tasked the Army with a review of the current body armor and soldier protection equipment industrial base and the outlook for future development and production.
 
“The committee asked for this analysis based on a concern that the end of large scale combat operations in Afghanistan would see the Army and Marine Corps scale back their requirements for, and funding of, body armor and other protection equipment.
 
“The briefing provided to Congress painted a mixed picture.  On the one hand, it showed that the Army has a solid plan to invest $176 million in research and development over the next five years.  The Army is also starting a new program, the “Soldier Protection System” to integrate new protective equipment.
 
“However, the briefing also pointed out that there is probably not enough funding in the budget for procurement of new body armor to keep the two current domestic vendors in production.
 
“How much additional funding is needed in Fiscal Year 2015 to keep both vendors in production? If we go down to one vendor, will that make it more difficult in the future to quickly ramp up body armor production if we need to – as we did at the start of the Iraq war?”
 
The officials responded that they believe it is very important to sustain an industrial base but are unsure of how much it will cost.

title: Fitzpatrick: Stop Cutting Workers’ Hours
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. ��� Congressman Mike Fitzpatrick (PA-8) joined the House Thursday in passing the bipartisan Save American Workers Act [H.R. 2575] which would increase employee paychecks and hours by restoring the 40-hour ��?full time��� definition which was changed by the president���s healthcare law.
���Everyone outside of Washington knows that ��?full time��� means 40-hours ��� only federal bureaucrats would try and redefine a commonly understood fact that is critical to millions of workers and employers nationwide,��� said Fitzpatrick on the House floor earlier in the week (watch). ���By moving the goalposts on what actually constitutes full time employment, this Administration fundamentally changed the workplace for hourly workers ��� increasing risk for lost hours and smaller paychecks as employers struggle to deal with the law���s provisions.���
Studies show that over 2.6 million Americans ��� primarily��the young, women, low-income earners and those without a college degrees ��� are especially at risk of having their hours and wages cut as a result of the 30-hour rule. The non-partisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) reports that passing the Save American Workers Act would increase wages for workers by $75 billion and let small businesses focus their resources on hiring more workers and growing their business by drastically reducing tax burdens found inside the healthcare law.
���By shifting the definition of full-time to 30-hours, the administration is adding another level of confusion to small businesses and their employees already struggling in this economy,��� said Fitzpatrick following the vote. ���With more than 70% of small businesses saying the healthcare law makes it harder to hire - and half saying they will either cut hours or replace full-time employees with part-time employees to avoid the employer mandate - Congress needs to come together and work and ease the squeeze on working families by restoring the 40-hour work week.���
���[The law���s] definition of full-time is counter to the traditional 40-hours of service threshold that most American businesses use to define full-time for benefits and other purposes. Implementing this new definition will require most businesses to change both their policies and their practices,��� wrote the Small Business Coalition for Affordable Healthcare ��� a group representing organizations like the National Retail Federation, Small Business Council of America, and Association for Manufacturing Technology (letter attached). ���Without H.R. 2575, employers will face higher employer mandate penalty taxes, and employees will see reduced hours and take home pay. The Coalition urges all Members of the U.S. House of Representatives to support H.R. 2575.���
James Hoffa, president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, has said the 30-hour rule will ���destroy the foundation of the 40-hour work week that is the backbone of the American middle class.��� Employer groups, including the National Federation of Independent Business, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, National Retail Federation and International Franchise Association have called the rule a major obstacle in job creation and have called for its repeal.
Similar, bipartisan legislation has been introduced in the Senate (Forty Hours in Full Time Act/S. 1188).
###
Congressman Mike Fitzpatrick is serving his third term in the U.S. House of Representatives. He represents Pennsylvania���s 8th district which includes all of Bucks County as well as a portion of Montgomery County. He serves as the vice chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations.

title: Rep. Black Speaks in Support of the Save American Workers Act of 2014
text:
(Click image above for video) 
Washington, D.C. – Today, Congressman Diane Black (R-TN-06) spoke on the House floor in support of H.R. 2575, the Save American Workers Act of 2014 – bipartisan legislation passed out of the House today that repeals the 30-hour definition of a full time employee in Obamacare for purposes of the employer mandate and replaces it with a 40-hour definition.  Below is a transcript of her remarks, or click here for video.
Mme. Speaker, Obamacare’s arbitrary 30 hour full time work week puts 2.6 million Americans making under $30,000 a year at risk of having their hours and wages cut. 
And 63 percent of those adversely affected by this arbitrary 30 hour rule are female workers, according to the Hoover Institute.
It’s no wonder that a majority of Americans oppose this law – and certainly no wonder that a majority of women oppose it.
For all the talk about the supposed “war on women,” it’s Obamacare that is waging a war against female workers.
That’s why I’m proud to stand in support of women across this country to repeal this arbitrary 30 hour full time work week.
Thank you, and I yield back the balance of my time.
###
Congressman Diane Black represents Tennessee’s 6th Congressional District. She has been a registered nurse for more than 40 years and serves on the House Ways and Means and Budget Committees.

title: PEARCE VOTES TO PROTECT AMERICAN WORKERS
text:
April 3, 2014 (Washington, D.C.) – Today, the House of Representatives voted to pass H.R. 2575, the Save American Worker Act.  Congressman Pearce, a cosponsor of this legislation, issued the following statement:
“The House voted today not only to reduce unnecessary and duplicative burden on thousands of small businesses nationwide, but also to protect jobs for those most in need,” said Pearce.  “Under Obamacare, full-time employment is defined as a 30 hour workweek.  Unfortunately, this change creates great conflict within the federal code, which will result in more regulatory burdens on small employers and threatens the hours and employment of predominantly low-income American workers.
“As a former small business owner, I know how burdensome the government can be on employers.  Congress and this administration should be focused on policies that incentivize employers to hire new workers and increase hours – not call into question the livelihood of millions.”
H.R. 2575 repeals the 30-hour full-time employment definition within Obamacare, replacing it with the standard 40-hour definition.  Without this simple change, the Hoover Institute estimates that as many as 2.6 million jobs are at risk of reduced hours if the 30-hour rule stays in effect.  The House of Representatives passed H.R. 2575 by a bipartisan final vote of 248 to 179.

title: Dr. Bucshon Votes to Protect Hoosier Wages, Hours at Work
text:
On Thursday, the House passed H.R. 2575, the Save American Workers (SAW) Act.  H.R. 2575 repeals the 30-hour definition of “full-time employment” in the Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as ObamaCare, and restores the traditional 40-hour definition protecting hourly wages for American workers.
Following the passage of H.R. 2575, Congressman Larry Bucshon, a physician from Southern Indiana, stated:
“I consistently hear from individuals, businesses, school corporations, and local governments here in the 8th District that they are struggling under provisions in the ACA.  One in particular, the 30 hour workweek definition, is estimated to put over 2.6 million Americans at risk of seeing their hours and wages cut.
“During the worst economic recovery since WWII, we should be helping Americans find work, not making it more difficult.  Unfortunately, the ACA puts employees at a disadvantage. It’s hard to find or keep a full-time job when the government penalizes employers for giving workers more than 30 hours of work.  How can hardworking Hoosiers care for their families when the ACA is putting jobs, wages, and hours on the line? It’s unfair and simply does not make sense.
“By repealing the 30 hour definition in the ACA, we are restoring the wages and hours the law puts at risk. This bill has bipartisan support in both chambers of Congress and from the American people. I sincerely hope the Senate will act immediately to send this bill to President Obama’s desk.” 
Yesterday, Dr. Bucshon took to the House floor during debate of H.R. 2575 to discuss the impact the 30 hour provision is having on 8th District school districts and to urge his colleagues to support the legislation.
Bucshon stated, “The vast majority of these employees already receive health insurance either through their spouse or other sources and many of them have worked for their school corporation for many years.”
He continued, “School Corporations don’t have the luxury of raising taxes to pay for these provisions of the Affordable Care Act. They aren’t a major business that can raise their prices.  School corporations simply can’t afford the Affordable Care Act. These Hoosiers work every day with students and because of this provision in the Affordable Care Act, our students will suffer.”
BACKGROUND:
H.R. 2575, the Save American Workers Act, passed with a bipartisan vote of 248 to 179.  More information on the bill can be found here.
In June of 2013, Bucshon joined the Indiana Congressional Delegation to send a letter to Health and Human Services Secretary Kathleen Sebelius warning that schools would be forced to cut workers' hours to avoid the ObamaCare penalty.
Examples of hours and jobs being cut in Indiana:
“Wolfe’s is one of countless small businesses, nation-wide, that will be forced, under the President’s current proposal, to streamline its workforce:  drastically reducing the number of full-time employees, and holding a vast majority of its work staff to a less-than-30-hours work week.” (WTHI; 6/25/13)
“Similar to other businesses across the country, Wolfe’s Auto Auction in Terre Haute says it is cutting work hours of several of its employees because of the insurance mandates of the federal Affordable Care Act…The reason cited? The Affordable Care Act defines a full-time worker as anyone who works 30 hours or more each week, and businesses will be required to provide health insurance to all of their full-time employees.” (TribStar; 6/25/13)
 “Fort Wayne Community Schools is trimming the hours of more than 600 part-time teaching aides and cafeteria workers in anticipation of a projected budget shortfall and to satisfy the requirements of the federal health care law, a school official said. Kathy Friend, chief financial officer for FWCS, said the school district is dropping 610 employees from 30 hours to 25 hours per week starting June 3, rather than provide them with health insurance as mandated by impending federal regulations.” (Journal Gazette; 5/27/13)
“The Affordable Health Care Act goes into effect next year, forcing employers to offer health insurance to any employee who works more than 30 hours a week. As a result, the Spencer County Commissioners are thinking about cutting hours for their part-time employees.” (14 WFIE; 6/10/13)
“The Vigo County School Corp. will no longer provide school bus transportation for middle school athletic events, starting with the 2013-14 school year…. The reasons cited are the Affordable Care Act and the need to reduce bus driver hours, as well as the need to reduce overall transportation costs.” (Tribstar; 6/16/13)
 “Greencastle Schools authorities have been wrestling with this question in recent months, coming to the hard decision to cut the hours of part-time workers to 29.5 or fewer hours.  The changes will apply to instructional assistants and kitchen assistants, a total of 54 GCSC employees.  As full-time workers under the new standard, the school would have to offer insurance to these employees.  Such benefits would come at a cost the school cannot afford.” (Brazil Times; 5/10/13)
“Lafayette School Corporation, where more than 150 of the schools approximately 600 non-certified employees have had their hours reduced to meet the federal definition of part-time.  ‘We cannot go out and raise the price of our product to assist us covering this.  We would have to go to the taxpayers and ask for some type of increase and I just don’t see that happening,’ said Les Huddle, superintendent.” (Courier Journal; 6/8/13)
“The Washington School Board…said many part-time workers may have to see hours cut to below 30.  The cut, Superintendent Daniel Roach said, was to fall under the proposed mandate of 30 hours.  Although the schools offer health care to the teachers, administrators, full time personnel and board members, the school will have to look at positions like substitute teachers, coaches and cafeteria workers to make sure they fall under the 30-hour-a-week minimum.” (Washington Times Herald; 6/20/13)
“Superintendent Ty Mungle explained due to changes in insurance provisions in the Affordable Healthcare Act, as of April 29 all members of staff that are not currently covered by the school’s insurance will be cut back to 28 hours per week.  Matt Roberts, president of the Eastern Greene Classroom Teachers Association, stressed to the board these series of changes are detrimental to the teachers’ dedication to the school system.” (Daily World; 4/8/13)
“Ninety part-time employees with the Fayette County School Corp. saw their work hours cut [the week of June 10th] due to a provision of the federal Affordable Care Act.  Hodges said 450 employees worked more than 30 to 35 per week.  The corporation does not offer health insurance to them.  The estimate cost is less than half of the fines the corporation would incur for not offering health insurance to those 90 employees, but is still a large sum, Hodges said.” (Indiana Economic Digest; 5/11/13)
“Womack [owner of IHOP franchise across Indiana] estimates the cost of [The Affordable Care Act] to his company will be 50 percent greater than his company’s earnings…’If the health care reform law is not repealed or if the employer mandate doesn’t go away, we’re going to have to take drastic action,’ Womack explains.” (The Foundry; 3/22/13)
”To prevent [Spencer County] from acquiring new full-timers, commissioners may opt to revise salary ordinances to reflect the new federal mandates under Affordable Care.  Kitchen workers’ schedules are divided into four-hour increments, with some working more than others…By consensus, they agreed to better divide duties and work about 28 hours each week.” (Journal-Democrat; 6/6/13)

title: Rep. John Lewis Says Government is Now Up for Sale
text:
WASHINGTON--Today the U.S. Supreme Court made a critical decision that will dramatically affect the quality of the electoral process in the United States.  The decision extends the damage the Citizens United v. FEC decision made to the integrity of U.S. elections by removing the cap placed on the number of campaigns to which one individual can contribute.
            Before the ruling one person could only donate a maximum of $2600 to a limited number of campaigns.  Now individuals must still abide by the $2600 cap to any one campaign, but they can contribute to as many political campaigns in one election or around the country as they would like. 
            The decision was sharply divided 5-4 with pointed dissent launched by numerous justices.  “If Citizens United opened a door,” said Justice Stephen G. Breyer during his dissent, “today’s decision we fear will open a floodgate.” 
Rep. John Lewis made these comments upon hearing about the decision:
                "Today the Supreme Court has declared that the federal government is up for sale to the highest bidder.  To suggest, as the Chief Justice did that, political campaign contributions can be likened to newspaper subscriptions, is an unfortunate comparison.  This decision tilts the balance of electoral power toward individuals with the deepest pockets, who after today have the power to influence as many elections across the country as they would like.
            "One man one vote is a sacred principle of our democracy.  The reason limits were placed on campaign contributions was to protect the integrity of the vote in this country, so that no one individual or corporation would have the power to override the public will or dictate the outcome of elections.  Today a series of Supreme Court decisions and state legislative actions are silencing the voices of the poor and the working class in the electoral process, and are giving the wealthy an unfair advantage over those who depend on the protection of the government the most.
            "It is important for the people to remain vigilant and struggle against these new devices.  As Martin Luther King Jr. said nothing can stop the power of a determined people committed to make a difference."
